Passage of the Department of Homeland Security funding package brings us closer to ending the reckless and harmful shutdown of DHS that Democrats triggered when they walked away from the bipartisan funding bill for the Department. That original bill contained new safeguards and oversight to protect the American public and our law enforcement, including additional funding for body-worn cameras and deescalation training.

Over the past five weeks, Republicans have made repeated attempts to reach bipartisan consensus to reopen the Department. Republicans offered proposals to expand the use of body-worn cameras; limit civil immigration enforcement in sensitive areas such as schools and hospitals; increase oversight of detention facilities; and implement visible officer identification.

While Republicans worked in good faith to try to reach agreement, Democrats remained intransigent and unreasonable with their list of demands.

Congressional Democrats have done real damage to the appropriations process by repeatedly forcing government shutdowns and refusing to fund entire agencies. Their refusal to fund ICE and Border Patrol leaves our borders and our country less secure and sets a precedent that they may one day come to regret.

Today’s action moves us closer to ending the disastrous shutdown at the Department, which has caused chaos at our airports, made us more vulnerable to cyber and terrorist attacks, delayed disaster response to communities in need, and caused thousands of hardworking federal employees to report to work with no guarantee of when they will be paid. Moving forward, I remain committed to ensuring adequate funding to secure our borders.

During Women's History Month, I would like to recognize a leader and humanitarian from Southwest Georgia, Lillian Gordy Carter.

Born in Richland, Georgia, in 1898, she quickly gained recognition in her community for her diligent work as a nurse.

"Miss Lillian", as she was known, served in her local hospital, challenged the bigoted color barriers of the time, and raised four children with her husband James Earl Carter.

She played an active role in her son Jimmy's senate, governor, and presidential campaigns, where she gained nationwide recognition for her earnestness and Southern charm. Much like her son, Lillian continued to serve the public long after her retirement. After completing her career as a nurse at age 68, Lillian joined the Peace Corps, where she worked in a clinic in India.

As a powerful figure for progress, Lillian inspired a president and continues to be an inspiration to generations that have followed. From Plains, Georgia, to Godrej, India, her compassion touched the lives of many.

Chairwoman Jennifer Porter of the Kootenai Tribe of Idaho represents a powerful legacy of leadership, serving as a third-generation leader for her family and community. With 32 years of dedicated service, she remains a steadfast champion for tribal sovereignty and a driving force in ensuring the Kootenai people have a safe, thriving environment to call home.

Her deep commitment to her heritage and her tireless advocacy for the future of tribal youth serve as a vital example of the strength Native women bring to our state. We celebrate her decades of leadership and her unwavering focus on the well-being of the Kootenai Tribe during Native Women’s History Month.

I am a co-sponsor of the bipartisan Native Women’s History Month resolution to formally celebrate the heritage and resilience of the 5.3 million Native women who have shaped our nation’s history. Their contributions must be honored as we continue working to uplift Native women across the country.

On National Vietnam War Veterans Day, we honor the more than 44,000 Vietnam veterans who call Idaho home and the millions who served with dignity and honor. To those who were not always given the welcome they deserved: we thank you for your service, we remember your sacrifice, and we remain committed to ensuring your legacy is never forgotten

Chairwoman Donna Thompson of the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes embodies the strength and leadership we recognize during Native Women’s History Month. With over 30 years of professional expertise—ranging from tribal accounting to her fourth term on the Fort Hall Business Council—she has been a steady hand and effective leader for the Tribal communities in Idaho.

From advocating for better funding for the Indian Health Service to her work in tribal education and agricultural development, Chairwoman Thompson brings deep expertise and a strong commitment to the communities she serves. Her commitment to the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes ensures a strong foundation for future generations, rooted in both cultural values and professional excellence.

I am proud to be a co-sponsor of the bipartisan Native Women’s History Month resolution to formally celebrate the heritage and resilience of the 5.3 million Native women who have shaped our nation’s history. When I first ran for State Representative back in 1992, my aspiration was to represent my hometown of Tarkio, Missouri. I was a twenty-seven year old farmer who just wanted to stand up for a way of life and his community.  I never could have imagined where that decision would take me.   

For 8 years in the Missouri House and Senate, I fought for Northwest Missourians. From deregulating vehicle inspections, to standing for chain gangs, to securing funding for rural schools in the desegregation fight, I never lost sight of why I was sent to Jefferson City. Then, in 2000, the good, hardworking people of Missouri’s Sixth District entrusted me to be their voice in Congress.    

For 26 years, I have had the privilege of serving, culminating in becoming the Chairman of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and passing some of the most significant legislation in our nation’s history.  The responsibility entrusted to me is not something I have ever taken for granted. Not for a single day.   

What I’m most proud of is the work my team did when Washington made life harder for the people of Missouri’s Sixth. Together, we stood with hundreds of thousands of Missourians in their toughest moments.  We helped them cut through red tape and navigate a system that often felt stacked against them.  We got them answers and fought to deliver real results when they needed them most.   

I’ve said all of that to say this: After considerable reflection, 2026 will be my final year in Congress.  This wasn’t an easy decision, but it’s the right one. I believe in making room for the next generation. It’s time to pass the torch and allow a new guard of conservative leaders to step forward and chart a path forward for Missourians.    

That doesn’t mean I’m slowing down, not even close.  As I enter the 4th quarter of my life, I have more left in me. As many of you know, I don't let grass grow under my feet. We’ve still got a lot of work to do. I’m going to fight to protect Missouri interests as we work to shape this year’s Highway Bill. I plan to finish this last term the same way I started, full speed ahead.   

Maintaining our strong democratic republic will always depend on good people stepping up to serve from every corner of our great nation. I’m grateful for my colleagues in both parties, for the people I’ve worked alongside, and even for the opponents who challenged me and made me better. Public service isn’t easy. It takes hard work, humility, a thick skin, and a willingness to fight for what’s right.   

At the end of the day, I’m still the farmer from Northwest Missouri. You’ll find me back home on the farm nearly every weekend, after all, it is planting season. In fact, I’ll probably be on a tractor this weekend. And come Monday, I’ll be heading back through Kansas City on my way to D.C. to keep doing the job you sent me there to do.   From the bottom of my heart, thank you.    

It has been the honor of a lifetime.

P000597.text:
RT by @chelliepingree: 🚨 FARM BILL POWER GRAB

The 2026 Farm Bill quietly slipped in three sections that could shield pesticide companies from lawsuits, block states from regulating chemicals, and weaken water protections nationwide.

Rep. Chellie Pingree just introduced an amendment to delete them entirely.

Here’s the plain-English breakdown everyone should understand 👇

1. Lawsuit Shield for Pesticide Companies (Section 10205)

If this stays in the bill, chemical companies could avoid liability even if new evidence shows their product causes cancer or neurological damage. As long as the pesticide followed the label approved under Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA), victims may lose the ability to sue.

Why this matters:

Bayer has already paid about $11 billion to settle lawsuits over the herbicide Glyphosate linked to non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma. More than 165,000 claims have been filed against Bayer tied to the product Roundup herbicide.

If Section 10205 passes, future cases like those could be blocked.

Pingree’s amendment removes that shield.

2. States Lose Power Over Pesticide Rules (Section 10206)

Right now states and local governments can create stricter pesticide protections than the federal government.

That includes things like bans on spraying near schools or buffer zones around homes and waterways.

Section 10206 would override those rules nationwide.

That reverses precedent set by the Supreme Court case
Wisconsin Public Intervenor v. Mortier, which affirmed that local governments can regulate pesticides.

Seven states currently allow local pesticide control.
Those protections could disappear overnight.

3. Weakened Water & Wildlife Protections (Section 10207)

This provision would exempt pesticides from additional review under major environmental laws including the Clean Water Act and the Endangered Species Act.

In practice that means pesticides approved by EPA could enter rivers, streams, and habitats without additional permits or environmental review.

Government monitoring has already detected pesticide residues in most U.S. waterways, raising concerns about runoff impacts on fish, wildlife, and drinking water.

Why This Fight Is Exploding

Critics argue the provisions protect chemical manufacturers, override state authority, and weaken environmental oversight.

Supporters claim the sections reduce litigation risk, simplify national pesticide regulation, and protect agricultural production.

Pingree’s amendment simply removes the three sections entirely, restoring the existing regulatory framework.

What Happens Next

The bill is still in markup inside the House Agriculture Committee.

That means these provisions can still be removed before the Farm Bill moves forward.

This fight will determine who controls pesticide rules in America — communities or chemical companies.

Key Takeaways

The Farm Bill includes three provisions that could shield pesticide companies from lawsuits.

They could also strip states and towns of authority to regulate pesticide use locally.

Environmental protections tied to waterways and wildlife could be weakened.

The Pingree amendment would remove those provisions entirely and restore current law. @amtoxicology @chelliepingree

RT by @RepMoolenaar: NEW REPORT | @ChinaSelect investigation exposes how the Chinese Communist Party is reshaping the UN to serve its own interests. 

Here’s what we found ⬇️

The PRC isn’t just participating in the UN system, it’s exploiting it.

Through money, personnel, and political influence, Beijing is working to remake the UN into a vehicle for CCP objectives at the expense of transparency, accountability, and democratic values.

Finding #1: Financial leverage = political power

China has rapidly increased its contributions to the UN, now second only to the U.S.

But these aren’t neutral contributions. Beijing is turning money into influence, shaping agendas, delaying funding, and pressuring outcomes to align with its interests.

In some cases, China has withheld or delayed funding to stall investigations it opposes, including human rights inquiries.

This is financial coercion inside a multilateral institution.

Finding #2: Staffing the system to shape it

Chinese nationals in UN roles have increased nearly 187% since 2005.

Beijing is placing officials in key leadership positions, especially in areas tied to development and the Global South, to steer decisions from within.

Some officials have gone further, advancing CCP priorities while serving in roles that require neutrality.
The result: erosion of trust and integrity inside UN institutions.

Finding #3: Peacekeeping as a strategic tool

China is the largest troop contributor among UN Security Council permanent members.

But deployments are not random, they are concentrated in regions tied to Beijing’s economic and strategic interests, like energy corridors and Belt and Road investments.

7/Under the UN flag, the CCP is able to expand its military footprint abroad while minimizing scrutiny.

This is the conversion of soft power into hard power, all under the banner of multilateralism.

Finding #4: “NGOs” that aren’t independent

The CCP uses government-organized NGOs (GONGOs) to gain influence in UN bodies.

Many of these groups are directly tied to the Party’s United Front system yet operate as if they are independent civil society voices.

9/ These entities have been used to:
▪️ Promote CCP narratives
▪️ Drown out criticism
▪️ Expand political influence
▪️ In some cases, engage in corruption and fraud

This undermines legitimate NGOs and distorts UN processes.

Bottom line: The CCP is executing a systematic, long-term strategy to reshape global governance, using the UN as a central platform.

Our report outlines steps to:
▪️ Restore accountability and transparency
▪️ Push back on CCP influence
▪️ Strengthen U.S. leadership in international institutions
▪️ Ensure the UN serves its core mission, not authoritarian agendas

The UN should reflect the principles of its Charter, not be repurposed to advance one country’s political system.

Read the full report and findings here: https://chinaselectcommittee.house.gov/media/press-releases/new-investigation-uncovers-how-china-controls-money-personnel-and-troops-at-the-united-nations

I am one of the few members of Congress who has actually passed a voter ID law (on a bipartisan basis), which I did as Speaker of the House in North Carolina, and that’s why I proudly co-sponsored the SAVE Act. While I support strengthening mail-in ballot integrity, many states like Utah, Florida, Alaska, and Montana rely on the use of mail-in ballots to conduct their elections, and we should not be completely upending how states already securely conduct their elections. Even if this issue is fixed, the SAVE America Act still will not have the 60 votes required to pass it.

While the so-called ‘talking filibuster’ has been floated as an option, there is a reason why previous attempts to utilize it in recent history have failed. A ‘talking filibuster’ would effectively make Chuck Schumer the new Senate Majority Leader, allowing Democrats to block every single Trump judge and executive branch nominee, and allow them to force endless votes on anything they want. Democrats would control the floor of the U.S. Senate until the end of the year.

There are only two ways out of a ‘talking filibuster.’ The first is for Democrats to miraculously give up and allow Republicans to pass the bill with a simple majority. That is never going to happen, and anyone who claims it’s even a remote possibility is either completely misinformed or intentionally misleading the American people.

The second way is for Republicans to substantially weaken or eliminate the filibuster altogether. I have made it crystal clear that I will never vote to do this. Eliminating the filibuster is a foolish and lazy idea pushed by politicians seeking short-term gain at the expense of causing irreparable long-term harm to our nation. Succeeding in eliminating the filibuster would significantly weaken the minority party, end the need for bipartisan compromise, and allow erratic swings in policy that would transform America for the worse. Those are just the consequences of a best-case outcome.

During the last Congress, all of my Democratic colleagues currently serving supported nuking the filibuster to try to pass their own partisan election reform bill. Democrats were dead wrong to try to change the filibuster when they controlled the Senate, and Republicans would be dead wrong to try to change the filibuster now that we control the Senate. The only real path to address the American people’s declining confidence in our elections is for both parties to find common ground on legislation that supports universal adoption of voter ID, proof of citizenship, and other vital election integrity measures.

F000466.text:
Each year, the Warrington Veterans Affairs Committee brings our community together to honor the Vietnam veterans among us—heroes of uncommon courage who answered their country’s call, served with honor, and came home carrying the burdens of war with quiet strength.

They are not distant figures in history. They are part of the living heart of our community—our neighbors, our friends, our family.

On Vietnam Veterans Day, and every day after, we offer what should never have been delayed: the full gratitude of a grateful community and a grateful nation.

To all our Vietnam Veterans, and the families who stood beside them, know that I will always work to ensure your sacrifice is remembered, your service is honored, and your place in the story of this nation is never forgotten.

Thank you to the 8th grade class of my Alma mater, Holy Family Regional Catholic School in Levittown, for visiting us in our Nation’s Capitol! 

Welcoming neighbors from our community to DC is always a highlight, and sharing this experience with students from my home parish made it even more meaningful.

As we approach our nation’s 250th anniversary, it felt especially meaningful to walk with the next generation of leaders through the very halls where generations have shaped the course of this great nation. Their curiosity, thoughtful questions, and unique perspectives were inspiring, and a hopeful reminder of all that lies ahead.

A big thank you to the outstanding HFRC team for continuing to help shape such exceptional service-driven young men and women of faith and character—we look forward to welcoming you back again soon!

Always great to be with my friends from the Bristol Borough Fire Association, especially as we celebrated both the extraordinary men and women who serve the Borough and a major step forward for the future of their fire service.

The BBFA is made up of some of the very best people you will ever meet—brave, selfless, dependable, and unwavering in their commitment and love for their community. Time and again, they answer the call and demonstrate their skill. 

Over the years, Bristol Borough and I have built a strong partnership rooted in a shared commitment to keeping this historic community safe and strong. That is why it was so special to not only recognize this year’s honorees, but also celebrate the $2 million I secured for the Borough’s new consolidated fire station.

This major investment will replace four aging facilities with one modern, centralized station — improving coordination, strengthening emergency response, and ensuring these outstanding firefighters and first responders have the support they need to continue serving at the highest level.

Congratulations to all of this year’s honorees, and as always, thank you to every incredible volunteer, President Steve Reeves, and Chief Herb Slack, and Borough Council for all you do for your continued partnership, friendship, and service to our community.

Join me in congratulating William Zaleski of Troop 27, from Coopersburg, on earning the rank of Eagle Scout! 

For his project, William helped transform Titus Elementary’s courtyard into a true outdoor classroom. Knowing the school had recently expanded its ability to teach outside, he set out to create a space that could fully support that opportunity. He restored the area from the ground up—cleaning the landscape, power-washing the shed, clearing and revitalizing the pond, and installing new benches that double as tables. The result is a renewed learning environment where students and teachers can step beyond the classroom walls and engage in a more hands-on, dynamic way.

Congratulations, William—and thank you to the entire PA-1 Scouting community for the mentorship and example that continue to shape young leaders through service.

Each year, the Congressional Art Competition offers a special look at the talent, creativity, and perspective of young artists across PA-1, and this year’s exhibition was no exception! What a pleasure to spend time with this year’s participants at the 31st Annual High School Art Exhibition at the Hicks Art Center Gallery, and celebrate the thought, originality, and heart behind each submission.

Congratulations to this year’s winner, Max Bollendorf of William Tennent High School, whose piece, “Apis,” will hang in the U.S. Capitol,  as well as every student who participated and made this exhibition such an amazing showcase of talent from across our community.

Arts and culture have always been an important part of what makes PA-1 so special, and it is clear that tradition is in very good hands. Investing in and celebrating the next generation of creative voices is how we ensure that legacy continues to grow and thrive.

As we move closer to celebrating America’s 250th, it’s important to remember the unsung heroes who helped shape our nation’s story.

One of those heroes is Polly Cooper of the Oneida Indian Nation. During the brutal winter of 1777–78 at Valley Forge, General George Washington’s Continental Army faced freezing temperatures, disease, and severe food shortages. Survival itself was uncertain.
 
Then came hope.
 
The Oneida Nation, steadfast allies in the Revolutionary War, traveled hundreds of miles to support the American cause. Among them was Polly Cooper, a woman whose strength, skill, and compassion would leave a lasting mark on history.

She taught soldiers how to properly prepare white corn, sustaining them through the harsh winter when many would have otherwise perished. She also tended to the sick, offering care and comfort in one of the army’s darkest hours.
 
In gratitude, she was gifted a black shawl, believed to be from Martha Washington, a symbol of deep respect and appreciation. Though history holds only fragments of her story, her legacy endures. 

Today, Polly Cooper is honored as a symbol of unity, resilience, and generosity, a reminder that America’s foundation was built not only by leaders, but by those whose names are too often left out of the spotlight.
 
As we reflect on 250 years of American history, may we never forget the heroes who stood in the gap when it mattered most.

On this day in 1923, Colonel Joe Madison Jackson, an American hero, was born in Newnan, Georgia.

After graduating from Newnan High School, Joe enlisted in the U.S. Army Air Corps, the predecessor of the U.S. Air Force.

Eventually earning the rank of Colonel, Joe Jackson served with distinction in World War II, the Korean War, and the Vietnam War. 

During the Battle of Kham Duc of the Vietnam War in 1968, Colonel Jackson demonstrated extraordinary courage by flying his aircraft through intense enemy fire to rescue three stranded servicemen.  For his bravery during that mission, Colonel Jackson was presented the Medal of Honor by President Lyndon B. Johnson on January 16, 1969. 

Colonel Jackson retired from the U.S. Air Force in 1974 after more than 33 years of honorable service to our Country.

Colonel Jackson will forever be remembered as one of the greatest Americans from Georgia’s 3rd Congressional District!

چەند ساتێک لەمەوبەر لەگەڵ سەرۆکی هەرێمی کوردستانی عیراق نێچیرڤان بارزانی قسەم کرد. 

پشتگیری خۆم بۆ بەرێزیان دووپاتکردەوە دوای هێرشە قبوڵنەکراوەکەی ئەم بەیانییە بۆ سەر ماڵەکەیان لە دهوک. ئەم پەرەسەندنە نیگەرانکەرانە ئاماژەن بۆ بەرزبونەوەی هێرشەکان دژی دامەزراوە عیراقییەکان، وەکو ئەو هێرشەی هەفتەی رابردوو کە بووە هۆی گیانلەدەستدانی ٦ پێشمەرگە، بەم بۆنەیەش پرسە و سەرەخۆشی خۆم ئاراستەی سەرۆک نێچیرڤان بارزانی کرد. 

سەروەری عیراق، لە چوارچێوەکەشیدا کوردستان، پێویستە بۆ سەقامگیری ناوچەکە. دەبێت هەموو کارێک بکرێت بۆ ئەوەی رێگری لەوە بکرێت عیراق پەلەکێش بکرێت بۆ ناو ئەم گرژییە. فەرەنسا هاوشانی هاوبەشە عیراقییەکانی دەمێنێتەوە.
